analysis.one_liner: Bans exports of US crude oil, gasoline, and diesel while the US military fights Iran, to hold down gas prices.
analysis.headline: One month after introduction, the bill has no cosponsors and sits in the House Foreign Affairs Committee with no hearings or votes scheduled.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would prohibit exporting American crude oil, gasoline, and diesel fuel for as long as US military operations against Iran continue, and until the President certifies that the Strait of Hormuz is fully open and global shipping there has resumed. The idea is that oil kept at home instead of sold abroad would increase US supply and lower prices at the pump during the conflict. The President could waive the ban for crude oil that American refineries cannot efficiently process, on the condition that it be refined abroad and shipped back to the US.
analysis.who_benefits: American drivers and businesses that buy gasoline and diesel, who would benefit from more fuel staying in the domestic market during a Middle East conflict that can spike oil prices. The bill text says the export ban runs from enactment until the President declares military operations against Iran that began in March 2026 have ceased and certifies the Strait of Hormuz is open and shipping has resumed [S2].

how_it_helps.text: Keeps US-produced crude oil, gasoline, and diesel in the domestic market instead of exporting it, which supporters argue lowers pump prices during a supply shock from the Iran conflict [S2].

Ties the ban's end date to concrete conditions: the President must declare the March 2026 military operations against Iran have ceased and certify that the Strait of Hormuz is fully open and global shipping has resumed, so the ban lasts as long as the supply disruption does [S2].

Includes a safety valve: the President may waive the ban for crude oil that cannot be efficiently refined in the United States, requiring such crude to be refined abroad and imported back, so US refineries are not forced to process crude they cannot handle [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Oil producers and traders who sell US crude and refined products abroad lose a major export market for the duration, and refiners that profit from selling gasoline and diesel overseas lose that revenue. US allies and customers that import American fuel could also face tighter supply, and a lower world price for US-bound barrels means lower revenue for domestic producers.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil exporters and refiners selling abroad

drawbacks.text: An export ban can cut into oil producer revenue and, by reducing exports, can weaken the dollar and world supply dynamics in ways that raise costs elsewhere; it also risks retaliation and leaves allied importers of American fuel short during a global supply shock [S2].

The ban on gasoline and diesel exports assumes fuel kept at home will reach consumers at lower prices, but refiners with export contracts could redirect sales domestically at market rates rather than passing savings to drivers; the bill contains no enforcement mechanism forcing lower pump prices [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill aims at a real pocketbook problem — pump prices during a Middle East conflict — and the crude waiver shows some care about refinery limits. But the mechanism is blunt: cutting off export markets punishes producers and refiners immediately, the benefit to drivers depends on producers and refiners passing savings through rather than capturing them, and the bill offers no enforcement to make that happen. It is a pressure valve of uncertain strength, and it never advanced far enough to be tested.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in May 2026 and referred to the House Foreign Affairs Committee, where it has sat with no cosponsors, no hearings, and no vote scheduled.

narrative.text: Rep. Brad Sherman introduced the bill on May 7, 2026 [S1].
It was referred the same day to the House Committee on Foreign Affairs, whose action history shows no further steps [S4].
No other member has cosponsored the bill [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has moved the bill or blocked it on the merits; oil producers and exporters remain unaffected because the export ban has not advanced, and drivers have seen no policy relief from it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil exporters, for now; drivers got nothing

for.name: Brad Sherman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the House Foreign Affairs Committee.

sides.party_line_note: With zero cosponsors and no committee action, the record shows no partisan pattern of support or opposition yet.

industries.note: The bill cuts off their ability to sell US crude abroad during the Iran conflict, lowering their revenue. Drivers' interest in cheaper domestic supply runs directly against exporters' interest in selling to higher-priced world markets [S2].

industries.industry: Refiners selling gasoline and diesel abroad
industries.note: The ban blocks their profitable gasoline and diesel exports, but the crude waiver keeping US-bound crude cheap could help refinery margins; their export revenue interest conflicts with drivers' interest in lower pump prices [S2].

analysis.trajectory: With no cosponsors a month after introduction and no committee action, the bill is almost certain to die quietly in the House Foreign Affairs Committee, as most single-sponsor bills do.
